changes.before: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
changes.after: Name an outcome using what was predicted and whether it was correct.

before: For a yes-or-no classifier, compare its prediction with a known answer. A positive prediction means the model says yes; it does not mean the prediction is correct.

Suppose positive means spam. A spam message flagged as spam is a true positive. A normal message flagged as spam is a false positive. Spam allowed through is a false negative. A normal message allowed through is a true negative.
Worked example: four messages have known labels spam, normal, spam, normal. Predictions are spam, spam, normal, normal. Each of the four outcome categories contains one message.

Read true or false as whether the prediction matched the known answer. Read positive or negative as what was predicted. Changing which class means positive changes the labels, so state the convention first.
Changed situation: A normal message is flagged as spam. With spam as positive, what is this?
The positive prediction was wrong, so it is a false positive.
after: A classifier puts inputs into categories. For this yes-or-no task, positive means predicted spam. Negative means predicted normal. Positive does not mean good or correct.
True means the prediction matches the known answer. False means it does not.
A true positive is real spam correctly flagged as spam. A true negative is a normal message correctly allowed through.
A false positive is a normal message wrongly flagged as spam. A false negative is spam wrongly allowed through.
You can count these four outcomes in a table called a confusion matrix. Always say which category counts as positive before naming or comparing the outcomes.
